meta.note: R15.2 quiz contract: items[].{id,nodeId,prompt,options[{text,explain}],correct,sourceRef?,source_ref?}. sourceRef is the in-page anchor; source_ref is the paper section, validated and surfaced as sectionRef. Authored from page content only — never invent values the page doesn't support.

items.prompt: SHD and SID both score an estimated DAG against the true one. What does SID count that SHD does not?

options.text: Ordered node pairs whose intervention distribution the estimate gets wrong
options.explain: Yes — SID counts the pairs for which the estimated graph fails to give a correct interventional prediction, which is why it can disagree sharply with edge counting.

options.text: Edges present in one graph but absent in the other
options.explain: No — that is SHD. It counts edge-level disagreement and says nothing about causal inference capacity.

options.text: The number of v-structures the two graphs disagree on
options.explain: No — the paper does not define SID in terms of v-structure disagreement.

options.text: The total variation distance between the two observational distributions
options.explain: No — SID is a purely graphical criterion; it never estimates or compares distributions numerically.

items.prompt: Why is SID called a *pre-*distance rather than a metric?

options.text: It fails symmetry — swapping the true and estimated graph can change the value
options.explain: Correct. The paper's own example is a non-empty graph versus the empty DAG: the empty DAG makes every set a valid adjustment set, so one direction is trivially 'correct' and the other is not.

options.text: It can take negative values
options.explain: No — SID counts pairs, so it satisfies non-negativity.

options.text: It is undefined when the two graphs are identical
options.explain: No — the paper characterizes exactly when SID equals zero; identical graphs are a well-defined case.

options.text: It violates the triangle inequality for CPDAGs only
options.explain: No — the asymmetry is the stated reason, and it applies to DAGs, not just CPDAGs.

items.prompt: For the running graphs G: A→B, A→C, B→D, C→D and H=G+(B→C), which pairs are wrong when the arguments are swapped to SID(H,G)?

options.text: Exactly (C,B) and (C,D), so SID(H,G)=2
options.explain: Correct — estimate G omits true H-parent B from C's adjustment set, leaving the direct back-door route to B and the fork through B to D unblocked.

options.text: No pairs, because G and H have the same skeleton
options.explain: No — H has the extra B→C edge, and swapping the truth role turns its omission into two intervention errors.

options.text: All 12 ordered pairs
options.explain: No — only source C has a mismatched parent set in this direction, and only targets B and D fail.

items.prompt: What problem does the equivalent graphical formulation of SID solve?

options.text: The causal definition is hard to compute, so SID is restated as a valid-adjustment-set check
options.explain: Right — the reformulation turns a statement about interventional distributions into a structural question that can be checked by walking paths in the graph.

options.text: It removes SID's dependence on the true graph
options.explain: No — the reformulation still asks whether a set is a valid adjustment set *relative to the true DAG*.

options.text: It makes SID symmetric
options.explain: No — symmetry is addressed separately, by the symmetrization extension.

options.text: It extends SID from DAGs to CPDAGs
options.explain: No — the CPDAG extensions are a different section; this reformulation is about computability.

items.prompt: SID uses the parent set as the adjustment set by default. According to the paper, why that choice?

options.text: It is easy to compute and depends only on the neighbourhood of the intervened nodes
options.explain: Correct — and the authors are explicit that this is a design choice, not a necessity: any other adjustment-set method could be substituted.

options.text: It is the only set that is provably valid for every DAG
options.explain: No — minimal adjustment sets are named as a valid alternative, so the parent set is not unique in validity.

options.text: It always yields the smallest possible adjustment set
options.explain: No — minimal adjustment sets are described as the *smaller* alternative; the parent set is not minimal.

options.text: It makes the resulting distance symmetric
options.explain: No — the choice of adjustment set is unrelated to SID's asymmetry.

items.prompt: What situation motivates a symmetrized SID?

options.text: Two DAGs where neither can be regarded as an estimate of the other
options.explain: Yes — with no ground-truth graph, the directional definition has no principled orientation, so the two directions are combined.

options.text: Comparing a DAG against a CPDAG
options.explain: No — that case is handled by the DAG-versus-CPDAG extension, which produces a lower and upper bound instead.

options.text: When the true graph contains hidden variables
options.explain: No — hidden variables are explicitly listed as future work, not the motivation for symmetrization.

options.text: When SID and SHD disagree about which estimate is better
options.explain: No — the paper motivates symmetrization by the absence of a ground-truth graph, not by disagreement with SHD.

items.prompt: Over what class of graphs is SHD defined in this paper?

options.text: Partially directed acyclic graphs (PDAGs), of which DAGs are a special case
options.explain: Correct — that is why one definition covers DAG-vs-DAG, PDAG-vs-PDAG, and DAG-vs-PDAG comparisons alike.

options.text: Directed acyclic graphs only
options.explain: No — restricting to DAGs would not cover the PDAG comparisons the paper makes.

options.text: Arbitrary directed graphs, including cyclic ones
options.explain: No — acyclicity is part of the definition.

options.text: Undirected graphs only
options.explain: No — SHD compares edge *types*, which requires orientation information.

items.prompt: The paper reports roughly quadratic/cubic timing curves but gives a quartic dense worst-case bound. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: The observations describe sampled graph families; the quartic result is a worst-case ceiling, so both can be true
options.explain: Correct — empirical average behavior over finite graph families can remain below an asymptotic worst-case upper bound.

options.text: The timing experiment disproves the quartic worst-case bound
options.explain: No — a finite average-case experiment cannot disprove a worst-case upper bound.

options.text: Sparse and dense SID have exactly quadratic and cubic complexity for every input
options.explain: No — those are approximate observed trends, not universal complexity guarantees.

items.prompt: Why does SID against an estimated CPDAG return lower and upper bounds instead of one score?

options.text: Different DAGs in the represented equivalence class can imply different SID values
options.explain: Correct — the bounds summarize the best and worst compatible DAG extensions.

options.text: The observational sample size is unknown
options.explain: No — the bounds arise from orientation ambiguity in the equivalence class, not sampling uncertainty.

options.text: SHD must be averaged with SID
options.explain: No — SHD is a separate comparison measure and is not part of these bounds.
